questions.stem: A marine biologist's tank controller compares a stored secret with the value typed into the keypad, and the team asks why every byte should be examined rather than stopping at the first difference.

options.text: A comparison that returns early takes a different amount of time depending on how much matched.
An early return leaves the unmatched bytes unread, so a later read may fault.
options.misconception: believes the concern is unread memory causing a fault

options.text: Comparing every byte lets the controller reuse the same buffer for the next reading.
options.misconception: invents a buffer reuse benefit for full comparison

options.text: An early return can only be used when the two values are the same length.
options.misconception: believes early exit requires equal-length values

questions.explanation: Early exit means the work done depends on where the two values first differ, and that shows up in how long the comparison takes. Unread bytes, buffer reuse and equal lengths are not the property that makes early exit risky.

questions.stem: An update verifier for the tank controller downloads the image, computes a checksum, and compares it with the value published on the vendor's page, and the owner asks what that proves.

answer.exemplar: A checksum confirms that the bytes downloaded match the bytes the vendor's page described, so a truncated or corrupted transfer is detected. It establishes nothing about who published that expected value, because anyone able to alter the download can alter the published checksum to match, and only a signature binds the expected value to the vendor's key.

questions.explanation: The check compares two values that may share a single source, so it proves consistency rather than authenticity. Detecting corruption is useful, but the publisher's identity stays unverified without a signature.

questions.stem: A biologist's lab tool compares two secret values and the team believes the timing leaks information about one of them, and asks why.

answer.exemplar: A comparison that stops at the first mismatching byte does less work when the values agree in their first bytes than when they agree in many, so the elapsed time carries a signal about the secret. A constant-time comparison always examines the same amount of data in the same order, so the time it takes no longer depends on where the values first differ.

questions.explanation: The amount of work done, and therefore the time taken, tracks how far the values matched, and that measurement is available to anyone who can time the call. Constant-time comparison removes the dependence by fixing both the work and the order.

questions.topic: A memory acquisition that loses the page file
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a memory capture does not hold the whole address space
questions.stem: A team argues that its memory acquisition of a tank controller captured everything the machine held, and asks an examiner to explain why that claim is wrong.

answer.exemplar: A memory capture holds only the pages resident in physical memory at the moment of acquisition, and the operating system moves cold pages out to the paging area to keep physical memory free. Any page that has been paged out therefore sits on the paging medium rather than in RAM, so without the paging file the capture is missing a portion of the address space and the analysis is incomplete.

questions.explanation: The address space is larger than physical memory because the operating system pages cold data out, and the capture only ever sees what was resident. Missing the paging medium means a portion of the address space was never acquired.
questions.hint: Compare the size of the address space with physical memory.

questions.topic: Adding a coverage-guided fuzzer to a build pipeline
questions.learningObjective: Explain how coverage guidance changes a fuzzer's search
questions.stem: A member asks how a coverage-guided fuzzer differs from one that simply feeds random data to the tank instrumentation target.

answer.exemplar: A blind fuzzer chooses each new input without regard to what the previous inputs reached, so most of them land in the same shallow paths and never explore further. A coverage-guided fuzzer records which edges the target executed and keeps the inputs that reached new edges, using them as seeds for mutation, so each generation tends to advance into code that earlier inputs never touched.

questions.explanation: Guidance turns the input choice into a search over the target's own structure rather than a blind lottery. Inputs that opened new paths are kept and mutated, so progress carries across generations instead of restarting from scratch.
questions.hint: What happens to inputs that reached something new?

options.text: The elapsed time grows with the number of matching bytes, so it leaks information about the secret.
The times are unrelated to the match length, because the comparison is already constant time.
options.misconception: assumes constant-time behaviour despite the rising times

options.text: The tool is slower on longer candidates, because it hashes the candidate before comparing.
options.misconception: attributes the increase to hashing the candidate first

options.misconception: dismisses a clear monotonic trend as measurement noise

questions.explanation: The durations rise monotonically with the length of the matching prefix, which is the fingerprint of an early-exit comparison. Hashing, jitter and constant-time behaviour would not produce that ordered relationship.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A secret comparison that returns on the first difference
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a timing leak allows byte-by-byte recovery
questions.stem: A lab's security lead explains how an early-exit comparison could let an attacker recover a reef controller secret one byte at a time.

answer.exemplar: If the comparison stops at the first mismatch and its duration reveals how many bytes matched, an attacker can vary one byte of the candidate at a time and watch the timing. Each attempt either extends the matching prefix or does not, so a few hundred thousand measurements can recover the whole secret without ever seeing a rejection message or a lockout.

questions.explanation: The timing turns the comparison into an oracle: a longer match takes measurably longer, so a candidate can be refined one byte per batch of measurements. Nothing has to fail or alert, which is what makes the channel so hard to notice.
questions.hint: A longer match means a longer measurement.

questions.topic: A sandbox whose default policy is permissive
questions.learningObjective: Explain what a permissive sandbox default means for analysis
questions.stem: A marine lab reviews its isolation tank and asks an analyst to explain what a permissive default policy means for the sample being run inside it.

answer.exemplar: A permissive default means any action not explicitly refused is allowed, so the sample's normal activity proceeds and the sandbox stops only the handful of behaviours somebody thought to list. That is the wrong way round for analysis, because the interesting behaviour is exactly what nobody anticipated, so a default-deny policy starts from a far safer baseline.

questions.explanation: Permissive defaults let the sample exercise whatever it likes, and the report then has to separate deliberate allowances from accidents. Default deny starts from the assumption that nothing is permitted, so anything observed was put there on purpose.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to an action nobody wrote a rule about.

questions.learningObjective: Identify where a taint rule loses a flow

stimulus.body: Tank log: I ran the taint rule over the sensor gateway. The rule flagged the value read from the temperature probe and followed it through the parser into the sample buffer. When the buffer is written out to the shared network share, the rule stops and reports the buffer as clean.

questions.stem: What does that log entry reveal about the taint rule?

options.text: It does not model the network write, so the taint stops at a boundary it cannot see.
The rule cleared the taint correctly, because writing to a share sanitises the data.
options.misconception: treats a file write as a sanitising step

options.text: The probe data is never untrusted, so the rule flagged it in error.
options.misconception: concludes the finding was a false positive without evidence

options.text: The rule cannot handle buffers, so its output for the whole gateway is invalid.
options.misconception: generalises one boundary gap into a total failure

questions.explanation: The tracking ran cleanly into the buffer and stopped at the write, so the rule has no model for that interface and the flow disappears from the report. That is an analysis gap rather than a sanitisation or a false positive.
questions.hint: Look at the exact point where the tracking stopped.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A memory acquisition that loses the page file
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the paging file matters during a memory capture
questions.stem: An examiner is asked to explain why the paging file of a controller matters when memory is captured from a running machine.

answer.exemplar: Physical memory is only a portion of the address space, and the operating system moves pages that are not being used out to the paging area to keep free memory available. Those paged-out pages are still part of the process's address space, so a capture that excludes the paging file is missing them, and any data that had been paged out is simply absent from the evidence.

questions.explanation: The operating system continuously moves cold pages out of RAM, so part of the address space lives on the paging medium at any moment. Excluding it leaves a gap that no other acquisition step covers.
questions.hint: Think about where cold pages go when RAM is needed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Adding a coverage-guided fuzzer to a build pipeline
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a nightly coverage-guided fuzz run can miss defects
questions.stem: A team adds a coverage-guided fuzzer to its build pipeline and a reviewer asks why the nightly run may find less than the team expects.

answer.exemplar: A nightly run sees one configuration of the code and one set of inputs, and any defect that needs a particular build flag, environment or input shape to be reachable is simply not in front of it. Coverage guidance improves the search within what the harness can reach, so the pipeline has to make sure the fuzzer is pointed at the configurations that matter, or it will report a clean run that says very little.

questions.explanation: Guidance is only as good as the reachable surface, and a single nightly configuration exposes a narrow slice of it. The fix is to point the fuzzer at the variants that matter rather than to expect one run to cover everything.
questions.hint: What does a single nightly run never reach?

options.text: The secret is now protected by encryption, because the comparison no longer varies.
options.misconception: confuses timing resistance with encryption

options.text: The comparison now uses more memory, which is why the duration is stable.
options.misconception: attributes stable timing to memory use

options.text: The candidate value is now validated before the comparison begins.
options.misconception: invents a pre-comparison validation step

options.text: The timing no longer depends on where the values differ, so the channel is closed.

questions.explanation: Equal durations regardless of the match position mean the work no longer depends on the values, which is exactly what closes the timing channel. Encryption, memory use and pre-validation are unrelated to what was measured.
questions.hint: What does equal timing across match positions tell you?

questions.topic: A secret comparison that returns on the first difference
questions.learningObjective: Calculate the time needed to recover a secret through a timing leak
questions.stem: A 24 byte secret is protected by a comparison that leaks one byte per 100 attempts, and an attacker can issue 5,000 comparisons per second. How many seconds does the attacker need to recover every byte of the secret?
questions.explanation: Recovering 24 bytes takes 24 times 100, which is 2,400 attempts, and 2,400 attempts at 5,000 per second takes 0.48 seconds. The leak is therefore practical rather than theoretical.
questions.hint: Work out the attempts needed, then divide by the attempt rate.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A sandbox whose default policy is permissive
questions.learningObjective: Explain why default deny suits an isolation tank
questions.stem: A marine lab wants its isolation tank to reveal what a sample would really do, and asks why a default-deny policy is the better starting point than a permissive one.

answer.exemplar: With default deny, the sample can do nothing until the analysts explicitly allow an action, so every observed effect corresponds to a deliberate exception and the set of possible outcomes is known in advance. With a permissive default, the sample exercises whatever it likes and the report has to separate deliberate allowances from accidental ones, so unusual behaviour is easy to overlook in a long log.

questions.explanation: Default deny makes the policy the reference point, so anything in the log was put there deliberately and can be accounted for. A permissive default buries the interesting events in a long list of unremarkable permissions.
questions.hint: Ask which policy makes the report easy to read.

options.misconception: treats the hosting page as proof of the download's origin

options.misconception: assumes an equal checksum means the vendor's own file was checked

questions.explanation: The verification compared two digests and established consistency between them, and one of them is a value printed on a page that could itself have been changed. Identity of the publisher and the safety of the content are simply not addressed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: Fixing a timing leak in a value comparison
questions.learningObjective: Assess whether hashing the values closes a timing leak
questions.stem: A team argues that comparing a hash of each value instead of the raw values closes the timing leak, and asks an analyst to assess the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: Hashing both values and comparing the digests largely closes the leak, because the comparison then concerns the digests rather than the secret, and an early exit over a digest reveals only a prefix match of a value that is not easily inverted. The reasoning holds only if the digest is not itself stored where an attacker can reach it, because a digest of a short secret can be attacked directly without any timing at all.

questions.explanation: The comparison argument is sound, since a digest hides the secret from the timing signal. The residual risk is elsewhere, in what the stored digest enables if the secret space is small enough to search.
questions.hint: Check where the stored digest sits before trusting it.

questions.explanation: The property an early-exit comparison lacks is a timing that is independent of the values, because the work stops where the values first differ. Lengths, storage types and repetition all work fine with early exit.

options.misconception: confuses allowed actions with attempted ones

The profile denied the three allowed actions afterwards, once the run had finished.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An update verifier that only checks a checksum
questions.learningObjective: State what a published checksum establishes
questions.stem: A lab member asks an analyst to explain what a checksum published next to a download tells you, and what it does not tell you.

answer.exemplar: A published checksum tells you whether the bytes that arrived match the bytes the publisher's page described, so corruption and truncation are caught. It does not tell you who produced that expected value, so if the same party can replace the download it can replace the published checksum as well, and the check will pass on a substituted image.

questions.explanation: The digest is an expectation, not a credential, and the party publishing it may be the same party serving the file. Catching corruption is worthwhile, but identity has to come from somewhere else.
questions.hint: Ask where the expected value came from.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A taint rule that stops at an interface it does not model
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a taint gap is worse than a false positive
questions.stem: A security reviewer argues that an unmodelled interface in a taint rule is more damaging than a false positive, and asks for the reasoning.

answer.exemplar: A false positive at least marks something for a human to look at, whereas a flow that stops at an unmodelled interface leaves later code believing the value is safe, and nothing in the report points at the place where tracking was lost. The result is a silent gap: the dangerous path looks like the cleanest one in the analysis, and the false negative hides what the review was for.

questions.explanation: A false positive costs reviewer time, while a false negative removes the very evidence the analysis existed to produce. The gap is worse because it is invisible in the output that people trust.
questions.hint: Compare what a reader of the report is told at each case.

questions.topic: A memory acquisition that loses the page file
questions.learningObjective: Explain why capture size does not measure completeness
questions.stem: A member asks an examiner why the size of a memory capture tells him nothing about how much of a controller's data was actually collected.

answer.exemplar: The size reflects the physical pages that happened to be resident when the capture was taken, and the address space is far larger than physical memory because the operating system pages cold data out. A large capture therefore says nothing about the missing pages that were on the paging medium, and a small one may still hold the interesting content, so the capture must be compared against what the paging area held.

questions.explanation: Size measures residency at one moment, not coverage of the address space, and the missing part is exactly the part the examiner cannot see from the capture alone. Completeness has to be established by reference to the paging area.
questions.hint: Ask what the size is a measurement of.

questions.topic: Fixing a timing leak in a value comparison
questions.learningObjective: Explain why fixed average timing is not enough
questions.stem: Why does a comparison that aims to close a timing leak need to examine every byte rather than merely taking the same amount of time on average?

options.text: Because a fixed average time still leaks the number of differing bytes.
options.misconception: believes matching the average removes the channel

options.text: Because hardware makes comparisons slower as buffers grow, so the average shifts.
options.misconception: invents a hardware timing dependency

options.text: Because the compiler may reorder an early exit, so the timing cannot be trusted.
options.misconception: blames compiler reordering for the need to check all bytes

options.text: Because an early exit varies the work per attempt, and only fixed work per attempt removes it.

questions.explanation: The danger is variation between attempts, not the average, so a comparison whose work per attempt depends on the values still leaks even if the average looks constant. Checking every byte in a fixed order makes the work identical on every attempt.
questions.hint: It is the difference between attempts that leaks, not the mean.

questions.topic: Fixing a timing leak in a value comparison
questions.learningObjective: Recognise a residual timing signal in measured durations
questions.stem: A lab records comparison durations for a 16 byte secret: 8,120 ns when the candidate differs in byte 1, 8,131 ns when it differs in byte 2, and 8,260 ns when it differs in byte 16. What does the pattern suggest?

options.misconception: judges a leak by absolute spread rather than by the correlation

options.misconception: treats near-equal timings as proof of constant-time behaviour

options.misconception: invokes a length effect although the lengths are identical

options.text: The duration tracks the position of the first difference, so the comparison leaks how far a candidate matched.

questions.explanation: The durations rise with the position of the first mismatch, which is the signature of an early exit, and the spread matters less than the ordering. Close timings and identical candidate lengths rule out the alternative explanations offered.
questions.hint: Look at the ordering of the three numbers.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A secret comparison that returns on the first difference
questions.learningObjective: State why a secret comparison must not exit early
questions.stem: A new lab technician is asked to state what makes a secret comparison unsafe to exit early.

answer.exemplar: A secret comparison that returns as soon as it finds a difference performs less work when the candidate matches the secret for longer, so its duration becomes a signal about the secret. If the timing can be measured, an attacker can use that signal to search for the secret a byte at a time, which is why the comparison must do a fixed amount of work regardless of the values it is given.

questions.explanation: The work done, and therefore the time taken, tracks how much of the secret a candidate matched, and timing is measurable by anyone who can call the function. Fixing the work per attempt removes that dependence.
questions.hint: Think about how much work the comparison does.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A sandbox whose default policy is permissive
questions.learningObjective: Compare default-deny and default-allow sandbox policies
questions.stem: How does a default-deny sandbox policy differ from a default-allow one in the way it constrains a sample?

options.text: Default deny still permits every action, but it records each one for later review.
options.misconception: turns default deny into logging with no restriction

options.text: Default deny blocks all actions, including the ones the analysts explicitly allow.
options.misconception: makes default deny absolute with no exceptions

options.text: The two policies behave identically once the deny rules are written down.
options.misconception: claims explicit rules erase the difference between defaults

options.text: Default deny permits only what is explicitly allowed, so nothing happens by accident.

questions.explanation: Default deny makes permission the exception, so an action happens only because someone allowed it, which keeps the results attributable. Default allow does the opposite and lets unlisted behaviour proceed unnoticed.
questions.hint: Ask what happens to an action nobody allowed.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: An update verifier that only checks a checksum
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a checksum cannot establish the publisher's identity
questions.stem: A lab member asks an analyst to explain why a checksum comparison cannot establish that a downloaded update came from the vendor.

answer.exemplar: The checksum is only a digest of the file, and to use it as an expectation someone must publish that digest somewhere the downloader can read. Whoever can replace the download can replace the published digest with a matching one, so the check proves internal consistency between two values that may share a single source, and never the identity of the publisher.

questions.explanation: The expectation and the file can both be controlled by the same party, so agreement between them carries no information about who made them. Identity requires a value the downloader can trust independently, such as a signature.
questions.hint: Ask who could control both sides of the comparison.

questions.subject: CYBERSECURITY
questions.topic: A signature that covers only the archive
questions.learningObjective: State accurately what a manifest-only signature guarantees
questions.stem: Which statement about a signature that covers only an archive's manifest is accurate?

options.text: It authenticates every file in the archive, since the manifest lists them all.
options.misconception: assumes listing files in a signed manifest authenticates them

options.text: It authenticates the manifest only, so files it does not list or describe are outside the guarantee.
It is useless, because a signature over a manifest cannot protect any file.
options.misconception: overstates the weakness to the point of total uselessness

options.text: It protects the archive as a whole, because the archive cannot be altered without the manifest failing.
options.misconception: assumes the manifest binds the archive contents

questions.explanation: A signature guarantees the bytes it covers and whatever assertions those bytes make, which for a manifest means the manifest's own description of the release. Files it does not describe are simply not part of the guarantee, and the archive as a whole is not bound by it.
questions.hint: Ask precisely what the signed bytes are.
